review_text: Kauffman is an incredible professor and 216 is pretty easy with him. His lectures are incredibly detailed and informative. The structure of the class is very well made and makes it easy to understand everything. Every assignment given gives enough practice for the exams (you should not chatgpt the projects for this reason) so you don't need to practice much outside of the coursework and if you didn't understand something in lecture the labs and projects will usually fill these gaps. The projects only have public tests and the exams are open laptop so you can download anything you want for the exam just no google or ai. One warning I'll give is he told us he would reorganize the grading structure to deal with ai cheating and his options were either lower project weighting and raise exam weighting, add an extra midterm, or automatically fail anyone who's exam average is below 70%. Personally I don't think these should be an issue due to what I've written in this review. If you're reading this and picking classes definitely take this guy over anyone else

review_text: Kauffman is so goated and beloved by all his students. He made content that I otherwise would've found relatively uninteresting (operating systems, unix processes, assembly) engaging. Exams are also tough but his homeworks and labs give you good practice for them. Most people probably don't actually do the homework but if you want extra practice then you should do it. He also gives opportunities for extra credit as mentioned in other reviews. I think there is no better professor you can take for CMSC216 and with Kauffman you'll be in good hands.

review_text: If you haven't already, go look at that rating and the amount of reviews. On god it is not a lie, he deserves it. When I tell you his class will be a detriment to your mental health and academic career I'm not joking. I'm going break down why though: 1. His teaching style is to essentially overload you with a bunch of information, most of which isn't relevant for the upcoming task such as project or test/quizzes. So while you're busy trying to sift through what you need and don't, along with trying to understand the topic at hand, he's already moved on to the next. Which is infuriating because I'm paying thousands of dollars for this to be my experience. 2. Remember what I said about this unnecessary things he'll teach in class? Yeah he'll make those small things important questions on his test/quizzes. 3. He will, and I mean will, overload you with work. The best way to put it, he operates as if his class is the only one you're taking. To give you an example, literally the night of our first exam, he assigned the next coding project and told us "I suggest you get started on this immediately". I got the notification for the assignment literally late night while me and a friend were studying for HIS exam that was going to happen later that day in Mckeldin. As you can image we were pissed. And he also gives little-to-no time between projects to breath. 4. Speaking of the projects, his project documents are longwinded and vague. So much so that the piazza is littered with people asking for clarification on things that should be crystal clear constantly. And you can get a bunch of points docked if you miss just 1 of the several details he gives you in his, on average, 7 page docs. Which if you ask me, it makes no sense that you have a doc that long and people in droves are still asking for basic clarification. You wrote all that for nothing then. 5. The TAs are hit or miss, and it's almost dramatic. Some are really cool and helpful, while others feel as if they think just being there while offering little to no should guarantee them a check. I had to hassle one of them to tell me what was wrong with my code for like an hour as I obviously didn't know and tried almost everything at that point. And once they finally helped me, it took them like 10 minutes to find the issue and relay it to me. There has also been multiply times where TAs will change their hours without updating the google calendar, and as a commuter it's just rage inducing. And I've brought this to Yoon's attention before and he acts as if it's a trivial matter. Like bro I'm wasting gas and time and he's so tight with his deadlines it makes no sense that he's chill about this. (Now the TA thing isn't that important since they're subject to change, but considering he chooses who becomes his TA, I think it's still worth mentioning). 6. His late policy. I don't think it's bad but I think it's worth mentioning and from here you can decide whether you're cool with it. So essentially you can turn in a assignment late only 24 hours after it's initial due date. So if it wad due the 21st at 11pm (yes all his projects are due at 11 pm, not 11:59pm), then the late due date is the 22nd at 11pm. And he will reduce the overall grade for this assignment by 15%. But don't get this confused with the GFA requirements, where if you don't meet them for each project you will be dropped by a letter grade. You can go back for any project to meet the GFA requirements (which could be to just pass all public test for example), but you won't get a new grade for that assignment. So if you get a 75% on that project, that's what you're stuck with. In all, please just avoid his class. It's unnecessary stress and I'd recommend that you don't pair this class with cmsc250. Take one or the other, especially if you can't escape his class for whatever reason (like me). And sure he has a seemingly nice personality and all, but if he was truly as nice as people say I don't think he'd work his students to the bone the way he does. It's needless and truly from my experience, I won't be able to say with confidence that I know how to code C by the end of this class since I and many others just understand enough to get the projects out of our faces and to get barely passing grades on his quizzes and exams. So if you want to actually know what you're doing, don't take him. GOOD LUCK!
label_rationale: Explicitly 'overload you with work'; projects assigned back-to-back; long vague project docs; points docked for minor omissions.

review_text: I took this course in spring 2025 and I can truly say that Fawzi was one of the best lecturers I've had at UMD. I learned so much from attending lecture and he explained topics very well. He would make explanations of topics very thorough and relatable so that they stuck. The discussions were not that useful in my opinion but that is very dependent upon your TA. However, the worksheets given in discussion proved to be very useful. Also if there was a problem that I could not figure out no matter how much I tried, I could always fall back on his answer key to point me in the right direction to start or learn how to do the problem entirely. Some might say that this "defeats the whole purpose of homework" but I would disagree saying that it made the homework less stressful and allowed me to learn something new rather than simply sitting there not knowing what to do. Overall his exams were very fair and were truly indicative of the content covered in class. Although he did not provide practice exams, reviewing the homework, worksheets, and lecture examples multiple times and ensuring that I was comfortable with those types of problems and the theory behind them was enough to do well. If you are on the fence about taking him, I would do it. If you attend his lectures, pay attention, and put in the work outside of class, you will do very well.

review_text: I think Teli is alright, but still a good choice for 250. He doesn't explain things very clearly, but he makes up for this by going through a lot of examples in depth during lecture. You're left with a strong understanding on how to answer questions correctly, but with hazy knowledge on why you format the steps in the way you're supposed to, especially since some of the TAs will format their proofs or answer problems a bit differently than Teli did. It's not a problem for most of the semester--the midterms are incredibly easy, easier than the practice exams. The content in the course only really gets difficult between the second midterm and the final, and since the final isn't cumulative, there's no easy content from the beginning to pad it; but still very doable if you study well. The quizzes are sometimes easy, sometimes difficult--definitely study for those, especially as you get further into the semester. Homeworks are challenging, so don't slack off on those either. Overall, the negatives of his lecturing style don't really show themselves until you reach the end of the course, and even then just skimming the recommended textbook helps solidify the things he doesn't go over as much. I complain about his lecturing style a lot, but honestly he is a solid choice for 250 and I would recommend; put in the work, and it's not difficult to get an A.

review_text: First, I'm just going to start by saying, for CMSC330, it really doesn't matter much who your professor is. The lecture quizzes, projects, discussion content, TAs, quizzes, and exam content are all exactly the same. The only difference between Cliff and Anwar's sections are which professor's lecture you can attend, but even then, you can just not go to lecture or go to the other professor's lecture (some people found that they didn't really like Cliff's lectures and attended Anwar's instead---the class is big enough that I don't think people would notice). Unlike CMSC351, the professor doesn't make that much of a difference for this class, so don't freak out too much. That being said, I do think Dr. Mamat has the better slides and also more experience in the field, so if you do have a choice, I would probably choose him. Here are my comments on the course in general (this applies for both Dr. Mamat and Cliff's sections): - All the class information is available here: https://bakalian.cs.umd.edu/330 - Literally 44% of your grade is free. Why do I say this? Projects make up 40% of your grade and you get around two weeks for each of them (give or take). You can ask questions, ask the TAs, look up documentation, submit as many times as you want, etc. within those two weeks. Each project took me between two and eight hours. There is literally no reason not to get 100% on every project as long as you don't procrastinate. The median on every project was between 97% to 100%. So again, there's literally no reason not to get 100% on every project, and they make up 40% of your grade. - 4% of your grade is lecture quizzes, which are completely open internet. You can run the code on your own machine, and the lowest couple of lecture quizzes get dropped. So between the lecture quizzes and the projects, 44% of your grade should be completely free (as long as you don't procrastinate). - The quiz medians were: Quiz 1: 14.5/20, Quiz 2: 15/20, Quiz 3: 17.25/20, Quiz 4: 16/20. You get access to all of the course's quizzes and solutions from previous semesters, which is helpful for studying. I honestly found the quizzes to be harder than the midterms. I will say, though, that I didn't do very well on the first two quizzes, but after that, I started buckling down and really studying and I got 100s on the last two quizzes. You'll be fine as long as you study and really understand the content. - 46% of your grade is two midterms and the final. The medians were: Midterm 1: 83, Midterm 2: 87.5, Final (with extra credit): 89.48. Just like the quizzes, you get access to every previous midterm and their answer key, and around ~85% of the content on these exams is the same every semester. They do change things up a bit sometimes (like I think we did more garbage collection than they did in previous semesters), but most of the exams cover very similar content to previous semesters, so it's really helpful to take previous exams for practice. And yes, there's extra credit too. - The discussions were fine. I didn't find them too helpful. There were good review questions, but they were all in a publicly-available GitHub repository that you could look at without going to discussion. Honestly, unless you're really confused about something, you can usually just look up your question online or on Piazza. There are a gazillion resources out there for Ocaml and Rust. For Cliff in particular, I thought his lectures are okay. He goes at a very manageable pace; definitely not fast by any means. He can get pretty theoretical sometimes. He answers questions well. TLDR; This is a fairly easy class as long as you don't procrastinate on your projects and do previous quizzes/exams as practice. I would recommend not starting the projects any later than the weekend before they're due. You could definitely knock them out over the weekend (if you don't mind working on the weekends). I thought the content was fairly interesting, although obviously that's extremely subjective and is up to how interested you are in this type of stuff. I would recommend taking Dr. Mamat but it really doesn't matter that much.
label_rationale: Detailed review explicitly describing projects/exams as easy and manageable; most of grade nearly free.

review_text: Terrible professor. He doesn't care about the class at all; he always came to class late, he never graded in a timely manner, when he released solutions to homework and practice exams they were almost always incomplete, and more than a few times outright incorrect. When answering questions, both in person and online, his answers are typically vague and unhelpful (he is also hard of hearing, so it will take some effort and some help from the people in the front row to get his attention). Going to his class is useless most of the time, just go do the homework instead. The second type was recordings taken of him delivering the lecture in a normal class, and these are much worse. The sound quality is terrible, there's a ton of awkward silences, he spends a lot of time answering questions from students who you can't hear, and they take about twice as long as the first type to cover the same amount of material. The homework is hard, but not as hard as understanding what it wants you to do in the first place. Logistically the entire class was a nightmare. He didn't give us a syllabus until the second week of classes. He made his midterms two hours long, which required booking different rooms to hold them in, which took him a ton of time to make work, which meant that we didn't learn the actual dates of the midterms until the week before. By the end of the semester he was well over a month behind on grades. Final grades were due on Friday, May 23rd, and we got them on Tuesday, May 27th. The exams are heavily based on the homework, usually copypasting the hardest problem from a recent homework and changing the numbers. Reminder again that they are two hours long. Just leaving this here: https://www.cs.umd.edu/classconcern Avoid at all costs.

review_text: As I am writing this, Justin's average rating on Planet Terp is a 4.69, which is even higher than Christopher Kauffman's average rating (4.63). I had Kauffman for CMSC216 in Spring 2025, and he was one of my favorite professors of all time. Needless to say, given all the hype around Justin, I had high hopes going into his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class. Now that everything's over, I can say in short that I am disappointed with my experience. To be clear, Algorithms as a Computer Science class is commonly agreed to be a terrible class pretty much everywhere (based on talking to many people from many different universities). A large part of this is due to the fact that those with minimal experience in algorithmic programming find the class extremely difficult, while at the same time those with a lot of experience in algorithmic programming (i.e. competitive programmers, like myself) often dislike how it is taught very mathematically rigorously yet with little intuition or application at all (in other words, this class will not get you through a coding interview). Yes, Algorithms, the Computer Science class, is more of a math class than anything else. Yes, Computer Science is not just programming, and Theoretical Computer Science consists almost entirely of pure math. All of this I knew going in. None of this prepared me for when I lost over half the points on a problem from Homework 1 asking me to prove the Big Omega of a certain function. I approached it as almost everyone intuitively would; like almost everyone had been taught to solve an inequality since middle and high school. Set up the inequality. Turn it into an equality, and solve the equality. Determine which side of the solution to the equality contains the solutions to the inequality, and turn the solution to the equality back into an inequality. Apparently, this wasn't rigorous enough for this class. Perhaps this is just how this kind of stuff works. But we were never told that solving it this way would lose us points, and the "correct" way shown in lecture seemed unnecessary and unintuitive. Instead, Justin complained that many submitted solutions to such Big-Omega or Big-O proof problems looked the way AI would solve them, and that such proofs "were generally terrible", citing several reasons why. Okay, fine. If you take Justin, make sure you explain the hell out of any answer you give to a problem. One problem on Exam 1 asked me to find a lower bound for something and to show my work. I later received minimal points for my answer, despite the fact that the work I had shown lined up almost exactly with a potential full-score answer as described in the rubric. Upon submitting a regrade request, I was told the grader had no idea what I did here at all, since I had no explanation at all. But the question never asked me to explain! Too bad. There was an Exam 1 MCQ problem which asked whether a certain algorithm was O(N^2) in the best case. The algorithm in question was O(N) in the best case and O(N^2) in the worst case. As such, most people in the class answered incorrectly, as technically an algorithm which is O(N) is also O(N^2). A big stink was made on Piazza about this being a trick question hidden in a sea of 50 multiple-choice questions, designed to make students lose points even if they understood the concepts it was supposed to be testing. One student asked, to avoid confusion, why didn't Justin instead ask if the algorithm was O(N^100) in the best case? Another student literally included a screenshot of the Merriam-Webster entry for "trick question" in their post. In the end, Justin's response was that technically the algorithm was indeed O(N^2) in the best case, and that he didn't expect his students to autopilot any questions in his class. On top of this, there was a question on the Exam 2 MCQ which, depending on your interpretation of the question (the wording was not specific enough), could have had two different answers. However, if you picked the wrong one, you had no recourse, not even through Piazza. By this point, people had long since stopped posting on Piazza about questions like this. They knew nothing would result from their efforts. On Exam 3, there was a free-response question which essentially asked us to find the shortest path between two points in "a simple, connected graph" (I'm simplifying greatly). Many test takers realized quickly the looseness of this wording and realized that, to cover all graphs which could potentially be described as "a simple connected graph", one needed to run Floyd's Algorithm, as a simple BFS would not cover the case of a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's would not cover the case of negative-weight edges. Once Exam 3 was graded, everyone who wrote such a solution to that problem lost points (there was a special "tier" in the Gradescope "rubric" for Floyd/Dijkstra solutions). I asked in my regrade request what the issue with my answer was. The response was that I needed to specify what my input to Floyd's Algorithm was or what graph I was going to run it on. I responded that in my answer I had specified running Floyd's algorithm on precisely the graph described in the problem statement. The response? "It does not define distances". Confused and a little frustrated, I wandered over to take a look at the official Exam 3 solutions. The official solution to that problem? Run a BFS. Justin is not the worst professor I've ever had (currently, that (dis)honor goes to Manoussos Grillakis). Justin is not the devil. Justin is not someone who you need to avoid at all costs. But as a student in his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class, I felt like the environment I was in was just a little bit more hostile than I was used to. Every time I made a Piazza post, I was just a little bit nervous that I'd get flamed by Justin in his response. I felt a severe lack of benefit of the doubt, almost to the point of actively trying to take away points from correct or mostly correct answers. Look. Everyone's different, and everyone is looking for different things in the professors they get. Lord knows I have some unpopular opinions regarding some UMD professors (both positively and negatively). You might enjoy Justin when you take him, or he might even have just been going through something this summer. All I'm saying is, if you do decide to take him (and, to be honest, given that the alternative is Kruskal, you might decide to take him anyway): don't say I didn't warn you.
label_rationale: Exams central to the course; grading described as strict/nitpicky with little benefit of the doubt.

review_text: Pros: dresses nice, review guides are very similar to the exams so if you diligently do them, you shouldnt struggle on the exams, the quizzes are free points so even though he doesnt tell us the content of the quiz, its simple if you do the homework(lowkey on depends ta tho, my TA was chill, I've heard that the other TA was lowkey bad). He posts the notes, with his voice recording over them, so if you miss lectures, it's not the end of the world. The best thing is that he curves graciously. The average for our second exam was 78; however, he wants the exam averages to be 83, so he curves them up to it. If you do poorly on an exam, these curves are lifesavers. He genuinely tries to ensure that we all do well in this class and listens to us. Cons: homework is pretty hard, I won't lie, but he also gives us a week to do them, and he encourages collaboration with your peers, just don't cheat on it. Regarding my grade, I don't study enough, which is entirely on me; nothing on him. Another con is that there may be gaps in your understanding due to inconsistencies in the notes. Since he is using other people's notes for this class, that may be the reason for these gaps, which could improve in future semesters, as this is his first semester teaching it. Final: These complaints stem from the fact that a 400-level math course is not easy. Shocker!!!. Just be prepared to do the work. He is 3.5, not a 4, but since there is not 3.5, I'm rounding up for my guy. Stop the hate!!!!!

review_text: I'm writing this review just after the final exam for Stat 400. It being his first time teaching at the university, Zheng started the year off rough, with confusing lectures, he was initially bad at explaining topics and gave no insight into what was going to be on each exam. After students expressed their complaints, he really cleaned up his act. For exam #2, he told us what type of problems would be on the exam and gave out practice problems similar to ones on the exam. He also began to give out extra credit points on the homework, which made it easier to recover points. For the final, we were allowed a double sided a4 sheet of notes, and he gave us in-depth practice problems that were very relevant to the problems on the final. I'm giving him a 4 star review because he really turned his teaching style around and doesn't deserve many of the 1 star reviews he was given by students early in the semester, when he was still acclimating to being a teacher for the first time. He also responds quickly to emails and is generally a pretty funny guy in lecture. Please don't shy away from taking his class because of the people who gave him low ratings early in the semester who were upset by their exam 1 results.
